title: NGO Affairs Bureau joins push to explain amended tobacco law
excerpt: The amended law widens smoke-free places, limits marketing and curbs tobacco firms' CSR spending, which could affect NGOs that take such money.
content:
Government agencies, including the NGO Affairs Bureau (NGOAB), met on 17 November to plan how to make people aware of the amended tobacco control law, The Business Standard reported. The global health organisation Vital Strategies organised the day-long workshop on a communication strategy for the Smoking and Tobacco Products Usage (Control) Act, 2005, as amended in 2026.

What the amendments do

  • Widen the places where smoking is banned
  • Restrict tobacco marketing
  • Curb the tobacco industry's use of corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities

Tobacco-related diseases kill 200,000 people a year in Bangladesh, the paper reported. "These changes won't mean anything if government officials and citizens are unaware of them," said Md Shafiqul Islam, a senior consultant at Vital Strategies.

Participants included Dr AKM Mamun Uzzaman, Director at the NGO Affairs Bureau; Sheikh Momena Moni, Additional Secretary (World Health wing) at the Health Services Division; Md Akhteruzzaman, Director General of the National Tobacco Control Cell; Md Mostafizur Rahman, Lead Policy Adviser at the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids; and Khaleda Begum, Director General of the Department of Films and Publications.

Why it matters

The bureau approves foreign-funded NGO projects, so its part in the campaign matters for the sector. The curbs on tobacco companies' CSR could affect NGOs and community groups that have accepted tobacco industry money for health camps, scholarships or tree planting. Health and youth NGOs also have a role in spreading the word about the new rules.

What to watch

Rules and guidance under the amended law, any NGOAB instruction to NGOs on tobacco industry funding, and enforcement of the new smoke-free places.
